\section[la ilusión]{la ilusión — excitement, hope; illusion}

\label{lesson:ES-C765-ilusion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to relive, then the Spanish for the diary.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la ilusión}
\textbf{la ilusión} — \textquotedblleft{}excitement, hope; illusion\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me hace mucha ilusión verte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am really looking forward to seeing you.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Me hace ilusión} — I am excited about it. It is usually a happy word in Spanish.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ilusión} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{illūsiō} \textquotedblleft{}mockery, deception\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{illūdere}, built on \emph{lūdere} \textquotedblleft{}to play\textquotedblright{}; Spanish turned it into hope and excitement.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la ilusión}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la ilusión}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la ilusión}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to relive, then the Spanish for the diary, then say \emph{la ilusión} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la ilusión mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Excitement, hope; illusion\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anhelar]{anhelar — to yearn for, to long for}

\label{lesson:ES-C765-anhelar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the diary, then the Spanish for excitement.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: anhelar}
\textbf{anhelar} — \textquotedblleft{}to yearn for, to long for\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Anhela una vida tranquila.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She longs for a quiet life.}
\end{quote}

Literary; in conversation people say \emph{desear mucho}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{anhelar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{anhēlāre} \textquotedblleft{}to pant, to gasp\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); to long for something is to be out of breath for it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{anhelar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{anhelar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{anhelar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the diary, then the Spanish for excitement, then say \emph{anhelar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does anhelar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To yearn for, to long for\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el capricho]{el capricho — the whim, the treat}

\label{lesson:ES-C765-capricho}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for excitement, then the Spanish for to yearn for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el capricho}
\textbf{el capricho} — \textquotedblleft{}the whim, the treat\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me di un capricho y compré chocolate.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I treated myself and bought chocolate.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Darse un capricho} — to treat yourself. \emph{Caprichoso} — fussy, impulsive.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{capricho} was borrowed from Italian \emph{capriccio} \textquotedblleft{}whim, fancy\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB). The Italian word is often explained as \emph{capo} \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{riccio} \textquotedblleft{}hedgehog\textquotedblright{}, hair on end, but that is not certain.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el capricho}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el capricho}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el capricho}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for excitement, then the Spanish for to yearn for, then say \emph{el capricho} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[aspirar]{aspirar — to aspire; to breathe in; to vacuum}

\label{lesson:ES-C765-aspirar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the whim, then the Spanish for imagination.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aspirar}
\textbf{aspirar} — \textquotedblleft{}to aspire; to breathe in; to vacuum\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Aspira a ser médica.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She aspires to be a doctor.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Aspirar a} — to aspire to. Also to vacuum: \emph{aspirar la alfombra}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aspirar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{aspīrāre} \textquotedblleft{}to breathe upon\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{spīrāre} \textquotedblleft{}to breathe\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
